entities.summary:
Pope Alexander III (born Roland of Siena, c. 1105–1181) presided over the Catholic Church as its head and ruler of the Papal States from September 7, 1159, until his death. His pontificate, one of the longest and most consequential of the High Middle Ages, was defined by a protracted and often bitter struggle for supremacy with Frederick I Barbarossa, the Holy Roman Emperor, and the resolution of the Investiture Controversy's lingering issues. Alexander III was a pivotal figure in consolidating papal power against secular rulers, asserting the Church's judicial authority, and shaping canon law, thereby profoundly influencing the institutional framework of medieval Europe.

Throughout his 21-year papacy, Alexander III navigated complex political and theological landscapes. He convened the Third Lateran Council in 1179, which enacted significant reforms, including requiring a two-thirds majority for papal elections to prevent schisms and condemning Waldensian and Cathar heresies. Militarily, he supported the Lombard League against Frederick Barbarossa, culminating in the Battle of Legnano in 1176, a decisive defeat for the Emperor, and the subsequent Treaty of Venice in 1177, which saw Barbarossa acknowledge Alexander as the legitimate pope. Alexander also canonized Thomas Becket in 1173, elevating the martyred archbishop to sainthood and reinforcing clerical immunity from secular jurisdiction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alexander III's decisive victory over Frederick I Barbarossa established the papacy's temporal and spiritual supremacy in Europe, solidifying its institutional power for centuries. His reforms, particularly the two-thirds rule for papal elections, significantly reduced schisms and shaped the Church's governance.
